instructional_purpose: Introduces the two repair systems Arabic applies to unstable segments: alternation of the weak radicals and outright replacement of a letter, and sorts weak-radical alternation into three types by phonological trigger. It also teaches where a weak radical survives untouched, so that learners stop treating each surface shape of a medial-weak verb as a separate lexical item.
concepts_taught: weak radicals as an unstable segment class
alternation type: loss of the weak segment
alternation type: conversion of the weak segment to alif
alternation type: relocation of the weak segment's vowel onto the preceding consonant
medial-weak verb behaviour across past, imperfect, jussive and imperative
retention of the weak radical in the base verbal-noun template
vowel colour on the first radical before consonant-initial past suffixes
replacement of an initial waw by the infixed t of the reflexive derived form
emphatic conditioning of that same infix
final-weak roots feeding a legal and religious noun vocabulary

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The surface shape of a weak radical is computed from the vowel it would carry together with the vowel on the preceding consonant, not memorised per word.
Three repair types are distinguished by trigger: deletion, conversion to alif, and vowel relocation.
A medial weak radical surfaces as alif in the base past tense when it and the preceding radical would both carry fatha.
The pre-alternation shapes cited for medial-weak verbs are reconstructions posited to motivate the rules; they are not attested surface forms and the derivation depends on accepting them.

The deletion rule is stated as applying to a weak letter at the end of a word, but every example given is a medial-weak verb whose final radical carries the jussive sukun; the rule statement does not describe the data it is applied to.
In the base verbal-noun template the medial weak radical is retained because it bears sukun after a fatha, which is a stable configuration.
Before consonant-initial person suffixes the medial-weak past stem shortens, and the first radical takes damma for waw roots and kasra for ya roots.
An initial waw in the t-infix derived form is replaced by t and the two identical consonants then geminate; the shadda therefore does not belong to the root.
When the first radical is an emphatic consonant the t of that derived form is realised as the emphatic counterpart.

The boundary between the two systems is definitional: one is restricted to weak letters and the other is not; traditions differ on which individual changes are filed under which label, and the lesson presents one filing as settled.
One of the verbal nouns listed for a waw-medial motion verb is lexically marginal and is presented alongside the ordinary one with no register or frequency comment.

The account of shortened suffixed past forms as vowel relocation followed by deletion is one analysis; a competing description treats it as simple shortening of a long medial vowel before a closed syllable.

recognition_criteria: a surface alif in the second slot of a base past-tense verb whose lexical root shows waw or ya there
a two-consonant past stem with a coloured vowel on the first radical plus a consonant-initial person suffix
a long vowel sitting on the consonant before the expected weak-radical slot in the imperfect
a shortened jussive or imperative of a verb whose imperfect shows a long medial vowel
gemination at the start of a derived form whose root begins with waw or with an emphatic
procedures: locate the weak radical's slot in the template
read the vowel it would carry and the vowel on the preceding consonant
select the repair type from that pair
for suffixed past forms, choose the first-radical vowel from the identity of the weak radical
before attributing a shadda to the root, check whether the root's first radical is waw or an emphatic in a t-infix form
conditions: conversion to alif requires fatha on both the weak radical and the preceding consonant
deletion is reported where the form would place sukun on the weak segment
vowel relocation applies where the preceding consonant is vowelless and the weak segment is vowelled
retention in the verbal noun requires the weak radical to bear sukun after fatha
exceptions: verbal nouns of the base template keep the weak radical although the corresponding past tense does not
final-weak roots yield participles and verbal nouns with their own shapes rather than following the medial-weak pattern
one motion verb is given two competing verbal nouns of unequal currency
contrasts: weak-radical alternation versus general letter replacement, by whether the affected segment must be weak
weak radical retained in the verbal noun versus converted in the past tense versus deleted in the jussive and imperative
waw-root vowel colour versus ya-root vowel colour in the shortened past
a shadda that comes from the root versus one that comes from a replaced then merged augment

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating the weak radical's fate as fixed per lexeme, so that whichever shape was learned first is generalised to all cells.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The repair is computed per form from its vowel environment, so one lexeme legitimately shows retention, conversion and deletion in different cells.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Ask which slot the weak radical occupies in this particular form and what vowels surround it before choosing a shape.

common_mistakes.pattern: Using the wrong first-radical vowel in the shortened past, most often carrying the waw-root vowel over to a ya root.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The residual vowel is the trace of the deleted radical and therefore encodes which weak letter the root has.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let the root's weak letter select the vowel: back vowel for waw roots, front vowel for ya roots.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assuming the verbal noun must show the same alteration as the finite verb.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The verbal-noun template places the weak radical in a vowelless slot after a fatha, which is stable and triggers no repair.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Derive the verbal noun from its own template rather than from the surface past tense.

common_mistakes.pattern: Collapsing the two systems and calling every letter change weak-letter alternation.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Replacement operates on non-weak letters too, including the augment of a derived form conditioned by an emphatic first radical.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check first whether the changed segment is a weak letter of the root; if it is not, the change belongs to the replacement system.

instructional_purpose: Teaches consonant merger as a conditioned, partly obligatory and partly blocked process, and trains the learner to read a gemination mark as evidence about morphology rather than as an unanalysable spelling feature. The register focus is formal legal and religious vocabulary, where merged forms are dense.
concepts_taught: merger of two consonants into one geminate
the merging segment versus the segment merged into
obligatory merger in final-geminate verbs of the base form
blocking of merger before consonant-initial person suffixes
merger and near-merger between phonetically similar but non-identical consonants
assimilation of the reflexive t-infix to a preceding identical or emphatic first radical
merger across word boundaries as an optional connected-speech phenomenon
reading a shadda as a diagnostic for root shape versus template shape

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Two identical consonants merge into one geminate when the first is vowelless and the second is vowelled.
In final-geminate verbs the merger is obligatory before vowel-initial endings and blocked before consonant-initial person suffixes, so one lexeme shows both a geminate and a separated stem.
The gemination in a t-infix derived form built on a d-initial root results from assimilation of the augment, not from a geminate root.
A shadda in a word whose root has three distinct consonants signals either an augment merger or a gemination-bearing template, and the two must be told apart before a root is assigned.
The lesson lists merged first- and second-person past forms as an optional variant and then, in its own error section, marks the same forms as wrong; the two statements are not reconciled.

Optional merger of a stem-final consonant into a following person suffix in the everyday standard register is presented as available; this is at best archaic or recitation-bound and should not be generated.
Merger across a word boundary between a word-final and a following word-initial identical consonant is a connected-speech and recitation phenomenon rather than an orthographic fact.
The pre-merger shape cited for a gemination-bearing noun places a vowel between the two identical consonants; this is a teaching reconstruction and not the shape standard treatments posit.
The jussive of final-geminate verbs is given with two options only; the fully separated jussive and the alternative final vowel are omitted, so the option set presented is incomplete.
The imperative of a final-geminate verb retains the geminate, in contrast with medial-weak verbs where the weak segment is lost.

recognition_criteria: a shadda on the final consonant of a short verb stem whose dictionary root repeats that consonant
the same lexeme appearing with a separated two-consonant sequence once a consonant-initial person suffix is attached
a shadda immediately after the first radical in a t-infix derived form
a gemination-bearing noun whose root shows a repeated consonant
an emphatic consonant followed by a geminate emphatic where the reflexive augment is expected
procedures: identify the two segments that would be adjacent before merger
check whether the first is vowelless and the second vowelled
apply the merger, or block it when the following suffix begins with a consonant
when a shadda is present, decide among a geminate root, a gemination-bearing template, and an assimilated augment before assigning the root
conditions: merger requires adjacency with the first segment vowelless and the second vowelled
the merger is blocked when the ending begins with a consonant, because the required configuration does not arise
assimilation of the reflexive augment is conditioned by the identity or emphatic quality of the first radical
exceptions: first- and second-person past forms of final-geminate verbs stay separated
the imperative of final-geminate verbs keeps its geminate although other irregular classes lose a segment there
cross-boundary merger is optional rather than required
contrasts: obligatory versus blocked merger within a single verb's own paradigm
a geminate that belongs to the root versus one produced by a doubling template versus one produced by augment assimilation
final-geminate verbs, which preserve their doubled consonant in the imperative, versus medial-weak verbs, which do not
identical-consonant merger versus merger of merely similar consonants, which is optional and register-bound

common_mistakes.pattern: Extending the merger to first- and second-person past forms.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: A consonant-initial suffix removes the configuration the merger requires, and the separated form also keeps the person marker audible.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let the shape of the following ending decide: vowel-initial endings merge, consonant-initial endings do not.

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading every shadda on the second radical as evidence of a doubling template.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: A root whose second and third consonants are identical produces a geminate for a different reason, and the two have different meanings and different derivational families.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check whether the root itself repeats a consonant before attributing the geminate to a template.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assigning a geminate root to a t-infix derived form whose first radical is d.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The gemination there is the assimilated augment, and the actual root's third consonant is a weak letter elsewhere in the word.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Strip the derived-form augment first, then read the root off the residue.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating a shadda as a single indivisible letter.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: It stands for a sequence of two consonants, and only by mentally separating them can the root and the template be recovered.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Expand the geminate into its two segments as the first step of any analysis.

instructional_purpose: Teaches the phonotactic ban on two adjacent vowelless consonants and the repair strategies Arabic uses when that configuration arises at a word boundary, together with the distinction between pausal and connected pronunciation that determines whether the configuration arises at all.
concepts_taught: the ban on two adjacent vowelless consonants
repair by inserting a vowel on the first of the two
repair by deleting a segment
repair by preserving or adjusting an existing vowel so the configuration never forms
pausal versus connected delivery as two pronunciation modes
the connective initial hamza and the word classes that carry it
interaction of indefinite nunation with a following connective hamza
the relevance of all this to recited and formally delivered prose

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Two adjacent vowelless consonants are disallowed and something must change when a form would produce them.
The default repair at a word boundary is inserting a short front vowel on the first of the two consonants.
The configuration arises only when the following word begins with a connective hamza, since that hamza is not pronounced after a preceding word.
The repair vowel is not uniformly the front vowel: plural markers and certain particles take other vowels in exactly this environment, and the lesson's default is presented without those cases.

The shortened jussive of the copular verb is explained as a cluster repair; there is no cluster in the cited environment, because the following word begins with a vowelled consonant, so the deletion is a lexically licensed option for that verb rather than a phonotactic repair.
The lesson's own error section states that a following vowel-initial word creates no cluster, which contradicts the deletion example it built on the same configuration.

The shortened variant is presented as an alternative recitation of a specific scriptural passage; a claim of that kind is a claim about transmitted reading variants and must be verified against reading-tradition sources before use.
The third repair strategy is illustrated with examples whose vowels are inherent to the words rather than inserted, so the illustration does not demonstrate a repair.
Indefinite nunation before a following connective hamza is resolved by vowelling the nunation's consonant.
In pause, final short vowels drop and indefinite nunation is not pronounced, so no boundary cluster forms.
Modern formal practice frequently avoids the configuration by pausing rather than by applying a repair, so written text underdetermines the delivered form.

recognition_criteria: a word ending in a vowelless consonant immediately followed by a word beginning with a connective hamza
imperatives and jussive verbs, which characteristically end in a vowelless consonant

an inserted vowel appearing on a word-final consonant that the citation form shows as vowelless

the following word must begin with a connective, not a stable, initial hamza

contrasts: connective versus stable initial hamza, only the first triggering the configuration
pausal versus connected delivery
insertion versus deletion as competing repairs
boundary cluster repair versus consonant merger, which the lesson explicitly separates

common_mistakes.pattern: Leaving an imperative's final consonant vowelless before the definite article.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The article's initial hamza is not pronounced after a preceding word, so its own vowelless consonant lands directly against the imperative's, producing the banned configuration.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Insert the repair vowel whenever a vowelless-final word connects to a connective-hamza word.

common_mistakes.pattern: Inserting a repair vowel where no configuration exists.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: If the next word begins with a vowelled consonant there is nothing to repair, and the insertion is simply wrong.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Test the following word's opening segment before applying any repair.

common_mistakes.pattern: Treating a stable initial hamza as connective.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: A stable hamza is pronounced in all positions, so it supplies the onset itself and no configuration arises.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Classify the initial hamza first; only connective ones drop and expose a vowelless consonant.

common_mistakes.pattern: Deleting consonants freely on the analogy of the licensed deletion case.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Deletion is restricted to specific lexical and morphological environments; elsewhere it destroys recoverable structure and the separated forms of geminate verbs in particular are governed by a different process.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Prefer insertion, and treat deletion as licensed only where a stored rule states it.

common_mistakes.pattern: Ignoring the choice between pausing and connecting.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The same written string is pronounced differently depending on that choice, and the repair is a property of connecting.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Fix the delivery mode before deciding what the boundary sounds like.

instructional_purpose: Teaches the template notation that represents any word as three radical slots plus additions, fixes the closed inventory of letters that may be additions, and turns the two into an explicit procedure for recovering a root from an augmented form. This is the letter-ownership machinery on which dictionary lookup depends.
concepts_taught: the three-slot template notation and what each slot stands for
radical letters versus added letters
the closed ten-letter inventory of possible additions, carried by a mnemonic
templates for the base form and its participles
templates for the doubling, hamza-prefix, n-prefix and s-t-prefix derived forms and their verbal nouns

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Any word can be represented by aligning its consonants with three fixed radical slots, with everything else counted as addition.
The set of letters that can be additions is closed and has ten members, memorised by a mnemonic phrase.
Any letter in a word that is not one of the three radicals must belong to that closed set, which supplies a verification test on a proposed analysis.
Each derived form has a fixed template for its verb and for its verbal noun, so the root can be read off mechanically once the form is identified.
A weak letter may be a radical or an addition, and only the template alignment decides which.
Each derived form carries a typical semantic function, so identifying the form supports a prediction about sense.
The count of ten additions treats the hamza and the long alif as separate members of the inventory, which is one conventional way of listing it.
The prefixed connective alif of the n-prefix and s-t-prefix verbal nouns is counted among the added letters when weighing the word.

The base-form section treats the short vowels and the participle prefix as the only additions, leaving the participle's long alif unaccounted for at that point although the later ambiguity section presupposes it.
The stated procedure assumes a unique template match; forms whose surface shape is compatible with more than one template are not addressed.

recognition_criteria: an s-t prefix, an n prefix, an initial hamza prefix, a t prefix, or an infixed t after the first radical, each signalling a specific derived form
a doubled second radical signalling the doubling form, as against a doubled final radical signalling a different one

a residue of letters that are all members of the closed addition inventory, confirming the analysis
procedures: identify the prefix, infix or doubling signature of the surface form
match the whole word to a stored template
align the three radical slots with the word's consonants
read the remaining letters off as additions
verify that every one of them belongs to the closed inventory, and reject the analysis if any does not
conditions: the procedure presupposes a triliteral root
template matching must precede radical assignment, otherwise a weak letter is assigned arbitrarily
verification against the closed inventory is what makes the analysis falsifiable
exceptions: a letter belonging to the addition inventory may nonetheless be a radical, so membership in the set is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for being an addition
the infixed t of one derived form sits after the first radical rather than at the word edge, which breaks the prefix-scanning habit

common_mistakes.pattern: Counting a prefixed t of a verbal-noun template among the root letters.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: That t is an addition belonging to the template, and including it yields a root that does not exist in the dictionary.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Match the template before reading radicals, and check the residue against the closed inventory.

common_mistakes.pattern: Assuming a weak letter is always an addition, or always a radical.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Weak letters occur in both roles, and the same letter can be a radical in one word and an addition in another.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Let the slot decide: if the letter fills a radical position in the matched template, it is a radical.

common_mistakes.pattern: Scanning only word-initially for the t of the infix form.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: In that form the t sits after the first radical, so an initial scan misses it and the first radical gets misassigned.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Look for the t between radicals as well as before them.

common_mistakes.pattern: Confusing the doubling form with the form whose final radical is doubled.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: They share the presence of a geminate but differ in its position and in meaning.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Locate where the doubling falls relative to the radical slots.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Verbal nouns of the derived forms follow fixed templates and can be generated from the verb without lexical lookup.
Base-form verbal nouns are unpredictable and must be learned per lexeme.
When the third radical is weak, the doubling form's verbal noun takes a different template ending in the feminine marker.
The form with a long vowel after the first radical has two verbal-noun templates, and the choice between them is lexically conventionalised rather than free even though both are grammatical.

The lesson first calls both templates of that form equally correct and later concedes that convention fixes the choice per verb; the two statements pull in different directions and the second is the usable one.
One of the paired examples given for the alternative template is not the conventional verbal noun of that verb, and the form cited would not be produced by a competent writer.
The alternative verbal noun offered for the seizure verb in the error section is likewise not a current form and is presented only to be dismissed.
A single root may host both a base-form verb and a derived-form verb with distinct meanings and distinct verbal nouns, so the two must not be substituted for each other.
The n-prefix and infixed-t verbal nouns are distinguished by which augment appears and where the short vowel falls, which is the main confusion point between them.

Identifying the template, extracting the root, and applying the form's typical semantics is presented as a reliable three-step decoding of unfamiliar technical terms; form semantics are tendencies and the third step is heuristic.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A four-radical stem belongs to its own class with its own templates, not to the triliteral derived forms.
The base four-radical past tense takes the same person suffixes as the base triliteral past; only the stem differs.

The base template's imperfect has a rounded prefix vowel and a front vowel before the final radical, while the reflexive template's imperfect has a low prefix vowel and a low vowel before the final radical.
The reflexive template converts a transitive base verb into an intransitive one whose subject undergoes the event.
The base template's verbal noun ends in the feminine marker and the reflexive template's ends in a consonant with a back vowel before it.

The lesson states that the noun formed on the long-vowel four-radical template is not a verbal noun of the base template; standard descriptions list that template as a second verbal noun of the class, so the exclusion as stated is too strong.
A stem with a repeated consonant pair is analysed as four distinct radical positions even where two are the same letter.
Reduplicated stems of that shape are treated by some analyses as reduplication of a two-consonant base rather than as four independent radicals; the lesson presents only the four-radical analysis.
Many members of the class imitate the sound of what they denote, which is offered as an explanation for why the class exists.

The class's greater phonetic weight makes it slower and heavier than triliteral verbs, and a classical poet exploited the transitive versus reflexive contrast to shift focus between agent and sufferer; this is a stylistic reading, not a grammatical rule.

Only the base and the reflexive templates are presented; the augmented four-radical templates and the class of triliteral stems padded to four consonants are not mentioned, so the inventory given is incomplete.

The passive participle cited for the hamza-medial member of the class is formed regularly but is rare in use, and the widely attested participle from that root belongs to a template the lesson does not cover.

instructional_purpose: Teaches the emphatic suffix attached to imperfect verbs and imperatives in its heavy and light shapes, the deletions its attachment forces on person and number markers, and the licensing contexts, chiefly oath formulas, in which it is required or permitted.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The emphatic suffix attaches to imperfect verbs and imperatives and never to the past tense.
Attachment is obligatory on an affirmative future verb introduced by the oath particle.
The light shape cannot attach to dual or feminine plural forms, where only the heavy shape is available.
Attachment forces deletions wherever a nasal of the person or number ending would collide with the suffix, and the residual short vowel preserves the identity of the deleted marker.
With a final-weak verb the weak segment is retained and the suffix attaches after it with a low vowel; with a medial-weak or initial-weak verb no special change occurs.

The heavy shape signals grim certainty and the light shape hopeful expectation; this affective mapping is the lesson's organising idea and is a stylistic reading rather than an established grammatical description, which distinguishes the two only by degree of emphasis and by distributional restriction.

That affective mapping is presented in the lesson as the stated conclusion of a historian about wartime speech; a doctrinal claim attributed to an unnamed source in a narrative frame cannot be carried forward as sourced.
A negated oath normally lacks the suffix because the negation itself supplies the emphasis.
The lesson does not state that the verb ceases to inflect for mood once the suffix is attached, so the interaction with mood marking is left unaddressed although the paradigm presupposes it.
The pausal realisation of the light shape, in which it is rendered as a long low vowel, is not covered, so the taught inventory of surface forms is incomplete.
The deletions are motivated by a general avoidance of consecutive identical or similar consonants at a word's end.

common_mistakes.pattern: Keeping the masculine plural marker before the suffix.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: That would stack a nasal against the suffix's nasal; the marker is deleted and only its rounded vowel survives as the trace.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Delete the plural ending, keep its vowel, then attach.

common_mistakes.pattern: Keeping the long vowel of the feminine singular before the suffix.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The same collision arises; the long vowel is deleted and its front vowel remains as the person trace.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Delete the long vowel, keep the front vowel, then attach.

common_mistakes.pattern: Using the light shape on dual or feminine plural forms.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: Those forms admit only the heavy shape, so the light one produces an unlicensed form.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Check person and number against the light shape's restriction before choosing it.

common_mistakes.pattern: Reading a verb-final geminate nasal as a feminine plural ending, or the reverse.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The two are distinguished by the vowel on the preceding consonant, and confusing them changes both the person and the meaning.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Read the vowel before the nasal: a low vowel indicates emphasis, a vowelless consonant indicates the feminine plural.

common_mistakes.pattern: Attaching the suffix to a past-tense verb.
common_mistakes.why_wrong: The suffix is restricted to imperfect verbs and imperatives.
common_mistakes.correction_principle: Convert to the imperfect before emphasising.

required_evidence: per occurrence: the underlying person and number of the verb before deletion, recoverable only from the residual short vowel together with agreement in the surrounding clause; and the presence of a licensing particle. The vowel before the nasal is also required to separate the suffix from the feminine plural ending, so an unvocalised token is frequently undecidable.

proposed_new_units.summary: A licensing and attachment table for the emphatic verb suffix: which contexts require it, which permit it, which persons and numbers admit each shape, what deletes on attachment, what residual vowel remains as the person trace, and how the result is told apart from the feminine plural ending.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-s09 covers clitic and pronoun layering, and this suffix is neither a clitic pronoun nor an inflectional ending of the ordinary paradigm; u-n01 covers case and mood but not a suffix that suspends mood marking. Neither unit expresses the person-and-number-keyed deletion table or the shape restriction, and without them a parser cannot recover the person of a suffixed form.
